catalog_quote: Given that register is not tone stricto sensu, and given that the register feature l in Drubea and Numèè is culminative (no more than one per stem), which is a property frequently associated with ‘accent’, one may hypothesize that Drubea and Numèè might be better described as accentual rather than tonal languages. I show in this section that this is not the case ... Neither of Hyman’s (2006) inviolable criteria is met: downstep is not obligatory in Drubea and Numèè, where many stems (and words) contain only registerless RBUs, that is, have no indication of register. Downstep is also not syllable-dependent: the RBU is the mora (although the syllable plays an important role in determining which mora in a CVV syllable is the RBU). new_statements.quote: Neither of Hyman's (2006) inviolable criteria is met: downstep is not obligatory in Drubea and Numèè, where many stems (and words) contain only registerless RBUs, that is, have no indication of register. Downstep is also not syllable-dependent: the RBU is the mora [...]. Finally, downstep in Drubea and Numèè is not demarcative, since it is found on both the first and second syllables of disyllabic stems; that is, its position within a stem does not seem to be defined or constrained by a reference to either edge of the stem. [...] Given this definition, Drubea and Numèè can be classified as bona fide tonal languages

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File (text extraction, lines 2163-2218 = article sec. 6.2 'Tone, register and the typology of word-prosodic systems', PDF pp. 39-40). The quoted passage is there word for word; the two '[...]' elisions cover (a) the parenthesis '(although the syllable plays an important role in determining which mora in a CVV syllable is the RBU)' and (b) the intervening sentences defining TONE per Hyman 2006: 229; the final clause continues ': their word-prosodic system is entirely based on a lexical pitch-based contrast which has a morpheme as its domain'. Surrounding section read: Lionnet raises the hypothesis that the culminative downstep might make Drubea/Numee 'accentual rather than tonal', tests it a…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Drubea is a tone (register) language: the word-prosodic system consists solely of a lexically specified downstep (traditionally 'low/marked tone' vs 'high') on a mora of the stem; at most one downstep per stem, but many stems have none, and in disyllables it may sit on either the first or the second syllable (three lexical classes /σσ/, /ꜜσσ/, /σꜜσ/), so its position is unpredictable and not edge-bound. The author explicitly argues this is not a stress-accent system. No opened source states where (non-contrastive) word stress falls; Gordon & Maddieson 1999 and the ALK likewise only say the language is tonal (two tones, low marked).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said about secondary stress in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: Recent loanwords from French/English form a fourth class with downstep always inside the initial long syllable (CVꜜV.CV(V), e.g. /oꜜoci/ 'horse', /kaꜜaʈɛ/ 'car'; §3.7 p. 27). Verbal classifier prefixes copy the register of the verb-initial syllable; compounds may contain more than one downstep. Utterance-final raising (Drubea) vs utterance-final downstepping (Numèè) are postlexical.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain of the lexical contrast is the stem/morpheme (register-bearing unit = mora); realisation described within utterances (pitch relative to the preceding syllable), with postlexical pre-downstep raising (upstep) and utterance-final effects. Analysis rests on Rivierre 1973 transcriptions (Unya dialect) plus the author's pitch tracings of Shintani's 1990s Païta-area recordings; the author collected no new data.
new_statements.identity_note: Lionnet 2025 describes Drubea (dumb1241) and Numèè (nucl1484) jointly as one word-prosodic system ('virtually identical', differing only in utterance-final phenomena); his Drubea data come second-hand from Rivierre 1973 (Unya dialect, north of Yaté) and from Shintani & Païta 1990 / Shintani 2019 recordings (Païta-area speakers). Gordon & Maddieson 1999 recorded speakers at Naniouni (west coast) and Unya. Language names in the sources: Drubea, nraa/nââ drubea, Ndumbea, Païta, langue d'Unya — all dumb1241.

sources.locator: §6.2 'Tone, register and the typology of word-prosodic systems', pp. 39-40 of the article PDF (see also §3.6 p. 19 ex. (34) for the three lexical register classes of disyllables, and abstract/§1 p. 3)
sources.note: Whole article on the word-prosodic system: Drubea/Numèè are tonal (register-based) languages whose only underlying prosodic primitive is a lexical downstep on a mora; downstep is culminative per stem but not obligatory, not syllable-dependent and not demarcative (found on either 1st or 2nd syllable of disyllabic stems, lexically); §6.2 explicitly rejects an accentual (stress-accent) analysis. Recent French/English loans always have downstep in the initial CVꜜV syllable (§3.7). No statement about non-tonal stress placement.

sources.note: Second-hand history: Haudricourt established the existence of tones in the southern Kanak languages; Rivierre 1973 compared the three far-south dialects (Unya/Drubea kept its tone system); Rivierre 1978 on tonal inversion. Nothing on word stress.

sources.note: States (abstract, p.66; p.67) that Ndumbea 'is one of relatively few Austronesian languages that are tonal'; the paper covers vowels, consonants, the three-way coronal contrast and prenasalized stops; no section or statement on stress/accent (only a passing mention of 'tonal patterns' as an uncontrolled factor in duration measurements, p.87).
